newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mulls re-export of foreign rice as food aid.
newsitem.headline: Japan mulls re-export of foreign rice as food aid.

text.p: Japan said on Tuesday it was considering using foreign rice, which it is obliged to import under a world trade pact, as food aid for other countries.
Agriculture Minister Ichizo Ohara said the idea of sending foreign rice back overseas as aid was being considered as a way to reduce excessive domestic grain stocks.
But an official at the Australian embassy in Tokyo charged that this would be against the spirit of the 1993 Uruguay Round world trade agreement under which Japan agreed to open up its rice market.
"The thing is, we're now buying unnecessary rice," Ohara told reporters. "Should we dump the imported rice in the sea?"
"There's nothing wrong with re-exporting foreign rice to poor countries."
Ohara said Japanese rice would be included in the scheme, "But foreign rice should be a top priority."
He said the Agriculture and Foreign Ministries would start technical discussions on the idea.

Under the 1993 Uruguay Round world trade agreement, Japan agreed to gradually open its rice market and committed itself to importing 511,000 tonnes of rice during this fiscal year to the end of next March.
It has bought only 155,300 tonnes so far this fiscal year, mainly from Thailand, Australia and the United States.

"I believe Japan's commitment under the Uruguay Round was access for foreign rice to Japanese market," said John Sainsbury, an agricultural attache at the Australian embassy in Tokyo. "If foreign rice is not granted access and is re-exported as food aid, it's not the spirit of the Uruguay Round," he said.

Despite Japan's commitment to opening up its long-protected rice market, exporters complain that little foreign rice actually reaches shop shelves. Meanwhile, consumers remain faithful to homegrown types of short-grain "sticky" rice.

Japan's Agriculture Ministry has estimated that domestic rice stocks at the end of October -- the end of the crop year -- stood at three million tonnes, almost double the 1.61 million tonnes of a year ago.
Good harvests in the past two years have swollen stocks in grain warehouses across the country. A stock level of 1.5 million tonnes is considered desirable throughout the year.

Japan currently spends about 13 billion yen ($114 million) annually on food aid programmes under its Official Development Assistance, particularly for poor countries in Africa and Asia, according to the Foreign Ministry.

The government provides cash-strapped countries with funds to import food such as Thai rice, U.S. wheat and South African maize. It currently spends nearly six billion yen ($52.6 million) a year for the rice import scheme. ($1=114 yen)
